list.listitem: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) remains a clinical diagnosis, with electromyelogram as the best confirmatory test. C
Symptoms that correlate best with an abnormal electromyelogram include hypalgesia, abnormal hand diagram results, and weak thumb abduction strength. C
Effective conservative therapies include nocturnal wrist splints and yoga. B

Local corticosteroid injection (CSI) improves symptoms, function, and quality of life among patients with mild to moderate CTS for up to 6 months and decreases the need for surgery for up to a year compared to placebo. A
Benefits and risks of surgery compared to nonsurgical therapies are uncertain. B
NSAIDs, vitamin B6, and diuretics are not effective. B

background.definition: Carpal tunnel syndrome is caused by compression of the median nerve by the transverse carpal ligament within the carpal tunnel. This compression may impair motor and sensory functions of the distal median nerve.

list.listitem: In a 2013 report, the overall incidence was 2.3 per 100 person-years.
The incidence is higher in women (2.8/1000/year) than in men (0.9/1000/year).
The peak incidence is between the ages of 45 and 64 years.
In a 1961 to 1980 Mayo Clinic survey, the incidence was 1.0/1000/year, and was again higher in women (1.5/1000/year) than in men (0.5/1000/year).
In a Swedish study, the prevalence of median distribution paresthesias was 14.4%.
However, only 3.8% of the diagnoses were clearly CTS by clinical symptoms, and only 4.9% (1/3 of those with symptoms) of patients had electromyelogram abnormalities.
An estimated $2 billion/year.
Median days away from work for US workers with CTS is 28 days.
Patients with untreated CTS have a pooled utility estimate 11% lower than age-matched population norms, which has a detrimental impact on their health-related quality of life.
Patients with low socioeconomic resources were less likely to be referred for CTS surgery, which may affect their work options. CTS symptom screening may identify an improvable health disparity.
High-force/high-repetitive motion overuse
Greater than 40% idiopathic
Obesity (27% vs 11% for people with body mass index >30 vs <30; OR, 2.99; 95% CI, 2.25-3.73)
Metabolic disorders (hypothyroid) and pregnancy
Wrist fracture
Osteophytes
Inflammation
Infection
Prolonged wrist flexion/extension

Amyloidosis. Patients with prior history of CTS release who need a pacemaker may warrant work up for cardiac amyloidosis, as this cohort has a higher incidence of heart failure and amyloidosis diagnosis after pacemaker implantation

Increased carpal tunnel pressure leads to median nerve compression, which then leads to decreased venous blood flow in the nerve, impaired axonal transport, and impaired sensory and motor fiber function.
The average carpal tunnel pressure in patients with CTS symptoms is 32 mm Hg compared with 2 mm Hg in control patients.
Ultimately, vascular ischemia can lead to demyelination and permanent nerve impairment if the compression is not relieved.
Improving ergonomic workstations and decreasing repetitive high-force motions may reduce risk. C
Lower vibration exposure with improved tools or antivibration gloves may prevent progression of CTS symptoms. C
Weight loss may decrease the risk for CTS in at-risk industrial workers. C
CTS remains primarily a clinical diagnosis, with electromyelogram (EMG) as the best confirmatory test despite a 10% false negative rate. C
CTS symptoms correlating best with an abnormal electromyelogram include hypalgesia, positive or probable hand diagram results, and weak thumb abduction strength. C
Nocturnal paresthesias, thenar atrophy, Phalen's sign, and Tinel's sign have little diagnostic value. C
In comparison studies, EMG continues to have higher sensitivity (>85%) and specificity (>95%) than high frequency ultrasound (sensitivity 57%-89%, specificity 65%-97%) in CTS diagnosis.,,,C

Differential.Differential_Features: Neck/shoulder pain; paresthesias limited to thumb; weakness in C6 muscles; abnormal reflexes
Forearm pain worse than distal pain; no nocturnal pain
Rare; motor innervation to flexor pollicis longus impaired (can't flex distal thumb phalanx)
Tender to palpation over first dorsal compartment; abnormal Finkelstein's test

list.listitem: The National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) recommends at least one symptom of median nerve compression, and at least one objective finding, defined as a positive Phalen's test result or a positive Tinel's test result, decreased pin-prick sensation, or a positive electromyelogram for median nerve dysfunction at the carpal tunnel.
However, a systematic review found that Tinel's sign, Phalen's sign, and decreased pin-prick have low diagnostic yield.

The American Academy of Neurology, the American Association of Electrodiagnostic Medicine, and the American Academy of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation all recommend confirmation of median nerve compression by electromyelogram for a formal diagnosis of CTS.

Typical symptoms of CTS include numbness, tingling, and pain in the median distribution of the hand, from the palmar thumb to the middle of the fourth finger. Paresthesias may extend proximally to the forearm and even up to the shoulder.
Symptoms are usually worse with prolonged flexion and extension and may awaken patients at night. Prolonged cases of nerve impingement may cause thenar atrophy and decreased grip strength.

History of hand numbness alone is inadequate to diagnose CTS. Of the 14.4% of patients in a Swedish community survey complaining of median nerve paresthesias, only 4.9% (~30%) had an abnormal electromyelogram.

Symptoms most strongly associated with an abnormal electromyelogram include: hypalgesia (ie, decreased pain perception along palmar index finger compared to ipsilateral little finger), positive or probable Katz hand diagram results, (Image 1) and weak thumb abduction strength.
The closed fist sign, square wrist sign, and flick sign (Table 1) are promising but have been less studied than the above maneuvers.
Phelan's (68% sensitivity and 73% specificity), and Tinel's sign (50% sensitivity and 77% specificity) have little diagnostic value.

Although the true gold standard for the diagnosis of CTS is intraoperative evidence of elevated carpal tunnel pressures, an electromyelogram is the standard used in most studies. One study found a 10% false negative rate for the electromyelogram, while a Swedish survey found that almost 20% of asymptomatic control patients had an abnormal electromyelogram result.

Ultrasound was similar in accuracy to electromyelogram (78% sensitive, 91% specific) in one study but the reference standard was clinical diagnosis and the study design (case/control) would tend to inflate the accuracy of the test. Ultrasound is used more extensively in Europe for CTS diagnosis; several small European studies show that median nerve enlargement at the distal wrist crease correlates well with abnormal electromyelogram findings. A retrospective study of 206 wrists found a sensitivity of 91% for gray-scale Doppler assessing median nerve enlargement, and 95% for color doppler assessing intraneural hypervascularization. A cross-sectional study of 85 consecutive patients referred for EMG/NCS found that ultrasound was 85% sensitive and 83% specific for CTS.

High-frequency ultrasound has been proposed as a diagnostic tool for CTS. US abnormalities correlation to CTS include swelling or flattening of the median nerve or increased palmar flexion at the transverse ligament. Ultrasound evidence of decreasing median nerve size also correlates well with postsurgical improvement.
In comparison studies, EMG continues to have higher sensitivity (>85%) and specificity (>95%) than high frequency ultrasound (sensitivity 57%-89%, specificity 65%-97%) in CTS diagnosis.,,,

A comparison of ultrasound, nerve conduction studies, and the Carpal Tunnel Syndrome-6 validated diagnostic tool using latent class analysis (a statistical technique to estimate the accuracy of diagnosis in the absence of a universally accepted reference standard) in 85 consecutive patients found comparable sensitivity and specificity for all three tests.

The pneumatic compression test is currently being investigated as an inexpensive alternative to electromyelogram. The test is done by inflating a blood pressure cuff around the wrist to 100 mm Hg for 30 seconds, with a positive test recreating symptoms of pain, numbness, or tingling in the median nerve distribution. The pneumatic test is done the same way, with a pencil laid under the cuff but over the carpal tunnel to apply increased pressure to the median nerve.

A clinical prediction rule found that age older than 50 years, duration of symptoms greater than 10 months, history of trigger finger, constant paresthesias, and positive Phalen's sign in less than 30 seconds predict a poor response to nonsurgical therapy. This rule has not been prospectively validated.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the patient with suspected carpal tunnel syndrome.

Overall, using wrist splints less than 3 months for CTS does not show a significant difference in pain or function, although nocturnal or long-term wrist splints may improve pain. For patients who want conservative therapy, a trial of splinting is reasonable. B For patients who do not respond, see algorithm in .

Compared to placebo, local corticosteroid injection (CSI) improves symptoms, function, and quality of life in the short-term (3-6 months) among patients with mild to moderate CTS and decreases the need for surgery for up to a year. A
Compared to surgery, local CSI has unclear benefits and adverse effects. B
Benefits and risks of surgery compared to nonsurgical therapies are uncertain. B
NSAIDs, vitamin B6, and diuretics are not effective. B

A Cochrane review of 14 trials involving 994 patients found that local corticosteroid injection (CSI) is effective in improving mild to moderate CTS in the short-term (ie, improvement in symptoms up to 6 months, function up to 3 months, quality of life up to 3 months) and decreases the need for surgery for up to a year compared to placebo. Serious adverse effects are uncommon.
CSI appears to delay time to surgery in patients who do not experience relief with wrist splinting; however, 3 in 4 of these patients eventually request surgery.
A small RCT found no additional benefit performing a second CSI 8 weeks after initial injection compared to a single CSI.
A Cochrane review in 2024 found that, compared to surgery, local CSI has unclear benefits and adverse effects.
The level of relief from CSI may be comparable to or better than NSAIDs and splinting therapy at 8 weeks.
An injection 4 cm proximal to the distal wrist crease is effective at 1 month and 1 year, and may decrease the risk of complications by avoiding increased pressure within the carpal tunnel.

Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections may improve mild to moderate CTS symptoms in the short-term (3-6 months), but more trials are needed. An RCT of 26 persons with bilateral moderate-to-severe CTS, in which each wrist was randomly assigned to be injected with PRP or normal saline, supports the efficacy of PRP for up to 1 year.

The INSTinCTS (INjection vs SplinTing in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome) trial randomized CSI to night splinting (6 weeks) and found comparable pain and function relief at 12 and 24 months, but the CSI group had a higher rate of orthopedic referral and CTS surgery compared to the night splint group, making CSI the less cost effective treatment option.
Diuretics, vitamin B6, and NSAIDs did not relieve pain more than placebo.

Based on a Cochrane review in 2024, the benefits and risks of surgery compared to nonsurgical therapies are uncertain. It is unclear if surgery will benefit patients who find nonsurgical options unsatisfactory. The authors suggest future studies should improve methodological flaws in blinding and should randomize patients who find nonsurgical options unsatisfactory.

A Dutch randomized trial concluded that adults with CTS are more likely to achieve recovery after 18 months if they are treated with surgery (N = 468) than if they are treated with CSI (N = 466). Number needed to treat (NNT) was 7 (95% CI 5 - 11). The surgical group had more wound/skin problem needing treatment (14% vs 7%), while more steroid-treated patients reported changed hand sensation (72% vs 66%).

A Cochrane review of 28 RCTs found low quality evidence that endoscopic carpal tunnel release (ECTR) surgery may be as effective as open carpal tunnel release (OCTR) surgery in terms of symptom relief and improvement in functional status. However, ECTR may be better in improving grip strength, have less minor but not major complications, and may lead to a faster return to work (ie, 8 days shorter) than OCTR. Given the low certainty of evidence, these findings may change with inclusion of future studies.

Among patients undergoing carpal tunnel decompression surgery, it is unclear if using absorbable sutures is more beneficial than using nonabsorbable sutures for skin closure, based on a Cochrane review. The former has the economic advantage of eliminating the need for return visits for suture removal.
CTS surgery in outpatient surgey settings may results in 85% cost savings over operating rooms CTS procedures under general anesthesia.
Simultaneous bilateral CTS release is more cost effective than staged procedures.
Patients who opt for simultaneous CTS release return to work in 2.5 weeks compared to patients having staged procedures (6-8 weeks).
Yoga therapy (11 postures twice a week for 8 weeks) improved grip strength and pain but not nerve conduction compared with nocturnal CTS splints.
Acupuncture, laser acupuncture, exercise, chiropractic care, and magnet therapy did not show clinically meaningful benefit over placebo or control.
A Cochrane review meta-analysis of 29 studies assessing the benefit of splinting for a total of 1937 CTS patients found no significant relief of pain or function when worn < 3 months.
However, a single study of patients who used nocturnal wrist splints reported a higher rate of overall improvement (RR 3.86, 95% CI 2.29 to 6.51, NNT = 2).

The most recent Cochrane review also notes moderate-certainty evidence that patients may not derive additional relief for CTS symptoms or function when splinting is used in combination with corticosteroid injections, platelet-rich plasma injections, or extracorporeal shock wave treatment.
Post-surgical rehabilitation have unclear benefits.
Likewise, ergonomic positioning or equipment have uncertain benefits.
It is unclear if exercise and mobilization exercises help.
Studies of carpal bone mobilization (wrist bone manipulation by physical therapists) and ultrasound therapy for CTS are small with conflicting results, but suggest a small short-term benefit.
There is limited evidence from two small RCTs that therapeutic ultrasound may be more effective than placebo, but it is uncertain how this modality compares to other non-surgical interventions.
A systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 RCTs of extracorporeal shockwave therapy found improvements in symptoms and functional outcomes similar to those obtained with local steroid injections.
Low-level laser therapy is not supported by robust evidence.
Studies of biopsychosocial rehabilitation for repetitive strain injury have unreliable data with no conclusive support for its effectiveness.
Consider referring for surgery patients who have been unsuccessful with conservative therapy and who have had the diagnosis confirmed by electromyelogram.
Nearly half of CTS cases will resolve spontaneously without treatment over time. C

Predictors for failure of conservative treatment include age greater than 50 years, diabetes mellitus, duration of symptoms longer than 10 months, severity of symptoms, or an abnormal electromyelogram. C

Patients with symptoms for more than 10 months, who are older than 50 years, with constant paresthesias, an abnormal electromyelogram, a positive Phalen's sign, and impaired 2-point discrimination are less likely to benefit from conservative therapies.
According to data from clinical trials, CTS symptoms in half of untreated patients in the placebo group resolves spontaneously.
See algorithm in .
Be consistent and patient with nocturnal splints.
If symptoms persist, wear wrist splints during the daytime, as well.
Continue splinting during other treatment trials.
Avoid repetitive wrist flexion/extension activities.
If your BMI is in overweight or obesity range, weight loss may help decrease CTS symptoms.
If no symptom relief with splinting, talk with your doctor about a steroid injection trial.
If no relief with injection, talk with your doctor about CTS release option.
CTS is a common complication in pregnancy, possibly from fluid retention, with an incidence of 2% to 35% in pregnant women.
Symptoms usually resolve after delivery, but one series showed continued symptoms in 46% of women at 1 year postpartum.
Conservative therapy with nocturnal wrist splints is recommended.
CTS is rarely seen in children except in those with genetic diseases, such as lysosomal storage diseases.

algorithm.title: Carpal Tunnel Diagnosis and Treatment Algorithm.

cell.label: CTS suspected (numbness/tingling/pain in thumb, median 4th finger; hypoalgesia; positive or probable hand diagram results; and/or weak thumb abduction strength).
If symptoms are not classic, consider diagnostic electromyelogram or ultrasound. CTS confirmed?
Trial of nocturnal wrist splinting in neutral position.
If no improvement in 1 month, consider CTS injection or oral steroids.
If no response, consider yoga or carpal bone immobilization, or obtain EMG to confirm diagnosis and refer for possible surgical decompression if abnormal.

tr.td: Patients draw in the markings for pain, tingling, decreased sensation, and numbness on a hand diagram. Their diagram is then assessed as below for positive, probable, and unlikely distributions for CTS.
Test for decreased pain perception along the index finger compared to the ipsilateral little finger.
Measure the approximate width and thickness of the wrist.
The square wrist sign is positive when the thickness:width ratio is >0.7.
Test resisted thumb abduction (abductor pollicis brevis) by raising the thumb perpendicular to the palm.
A positive Flick sign is when patients flick or shake their hands to relieve hand paresthesias.
